source: Sobel, Tenenbaum & Gopnik (2004) pass rates as quoted in the 2018 PLoS ONE replication, Table 1 (variability in 2- to 5-year-olds' causal inference)
finding: The 2018 paper re-ran Sobel 2004 trials and prints the original pass rates next to its own. Most cells replicate. One backward-blocking cell does not.
numbers: Replication N=90 (23 two-, 23 three-, 23 four-, 21 five-year-olds; 25 excluded). Originals had n=16 per age cell. Indirect screening-off B: orig 100% (16/16) at 3y and 4y Exp1, 94% (15/16) 4y Exp2; replication 96% (22/23) at 3y and 4y. Backward blocking 3y: orig 50% (8/16) vs rep 70% (16/23), p=.32. 4y Exp1: orig 88% (14/16) vs rep 96% (22/23), p=.56. 4y Exp2: orig 63% (10/16) vs rep 96% (22/23), chi2(1)=7.04, p=.03, not matched. Screening-off at 2y: orig 72% (18/25, Sobel and Kirkham 2006) vs rep 57% (13/23). Backward blocking 2y 17%, 5y 100%. Gopnik 2001 own pass rates not reported there.
limits: Page read through a fetch tool that summarised the text; re-check table values in the PDF before quoting in print. Original cells have n=16, so intervals are wide (14/16 = 88%, 95% CI roughly 62-98%). Same research field, not a fully independent lab for every cell.
agent_relevance: Backward blocking is the step where later evidence discounts an earlier suspect (S5). It is reliable at ages 4-5 but cell sizes are tiny, so treat it as a design hint, not an effect-size anchor.

source: Griffiths, Sobel, Tenenbaum & Gopnik (2011) Bayes and blickets: effects of knowledge on causal induction in children and adults. Cognitive Science 35
finding: Adult and child blicket experiments tied to a Bayesian model with a base-rate prior. Adults match the model closely. Children match it only in direction.
numbers: Exp1 adults N=60 (5 base-rate groups), model-rating r=0.97 (Power PC r=0.325). Exp2 adults N=20 analysed, r=0.98 (Power PC 0.768). Exp3 4-year-olds N=16 (mean 54 months): proportion saying blicket A=.87, B=.63, C=.50, X and Y=.87. Exp4 adults N=24. Exp5 4-year-olds N=24: object B called a blicket 79% when the detector was probabilistic vs 8% when deterministic, t(22)=7.60, d=3.10. Sobel 2004 design cited: 2 or 10 of 12 objects activate (rare vs common).
limits: Authors say child data match the model only qualitatively and caution against concluding that children compute Bayes. Exp3 child cell is N=16. The page was read through character 200000 of 207955; Schulz 2007 and Kushnir and Gopnik do not appear in the part read.
agent_relevance: A prior that depends on the base rate of causes in the domain (rare vs common) changes the verdict on an ambiguous suspect. A scaffold can store 'how often do causes appear here' as a number and use it at S4/S5.

source: Kloos & Sloutsky (2005) Do preschoolers understand causality? A critical look. CogSci Proceedings 27
finding: An independent lab (Ohio State, not the Gopnik group) tested blocking logic with a two-phase paradigm. Adults separated causes from effects. Preschoolers blocked the redundant cue equally in both framings, so blocking alone did not show causal knowledge.
numbers: Exp1: 33 children aged 4-5 (mean about 60 months) and 27 adults; 13 more children and 3 adults dropped for failing the learning criterion. Interaction condition x age F(1,56)=6.37, p<.02. Adults differed by condition t(25)=2.53, p<.02; children did not, t(31)=1.06, p>.29. 82% of children differed from chance by binomial test. Exp2: 25 children aged 4-5, 11 dropped; check-trial accuracy .82 (prediction) and .89 (diagnosis). Same null.
limits: Not the blicket machine; uses cover stories (fruit, animal marks). Authors concede the diagnostic condition may be harder for children. A 2005 proceedings paper, not a journal article.
agent_relevance: Discounting a second cue (blocking) can come from simple associative competition. Do not read 'the agent discounted the extra variable' as proof of causal reasoning; test with a case where the cause or effect framing should flip the answer.

source: Beaton & Benton (2024) Dancing on the ceiling: the role of different forms of thinking on retrospective reevaluation in children. CogSci Proceedings 46
finding: A different lab (Vanderbilt) re-tested backward blocking in the blicket paradigm with a better control trial and training on how effects add. Four-year-olds blocked only after additivity training. Five-year-olds blocked in all conditions.
numbers: 26 four-year-olds (mean 54.4 months) and 33 five-year-olds (mean 65.3 months). 4y: condition x trial chi2(2)=8.14, p=.02; blocking in Additive chi2(1)=7.22, p=.01, odds ratio 62.03 (95% CI 6.67-18732.11); not in Ceiling (p=.10) or Control (p=.58). 5y: main effect of trial chi2(1)=25.24, p<.001, odds ratio 7.78 (95% CI 2.15-35.34) in all conditions. Condition effect on other objects n.s. (4y p=.18; 5y p=.16). 4y judgments fit an associative (delta-rule) model best; 5y fit the Bayesian model better.
limits: Very wide confidence interval for the 4y odds ratio. Model comparison is fit to few trials. Single study.
agent_relevance: Whether a 'discount the extra suspect' step fires depends on what the learner believes about how effects add. State that assumption (do causes add, or does one suffice?) explicitly in S3.

source: Sobel & Munro (2006) When Mr. Blicket wants it, children are Bayesian. CogSci Proceedings 28
finding: Restates the Sobel 2004 base-rate design: 12 objects tried one at a time, either 2 or 10 activate, then a backward-blocking test. Four-year-olds followed the base rate. Three-year-olds called B a blicket in both conditions. The paper extends the logic to desires in 3-year-olds.
numbers: Design numbers: 12 objects, 2 (rare) or 10 (common) activate. Per-cell pass rates of the 2004 study are not printed in the part read.
limits: Read the abstract and background of a 7-page proceeding. Does not give Gopnik 2001 pass rates.
agent_relevance: Confirms what the base-rate manipulation was; supports a 'domain base rate of causes' slot in the schema.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases (COLM 2025, arXiv 2505.09614v3) - models, reasoning effort, compute
finding: Tested GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3 and R1, QwQ, gemma3 (12B, 27B), llama3.3, llama3.2-3B, and o3-mini/o4-mini at three reasoning-effort levels. In the conjunctive 8-object setting, higher reasoning effort lagged behind lower effort and behind the oracle in exploration. The hypothesis-sampling agent was shown with gpt-4o.
numbers: Agent gets up to 32 actions, 4 or 8 objects, 2 blickets, at least 16 trials per model, prompt and system prompt. Hypothesis-sampling agent uses 16, 32, 64 or 96 unique hypotheses; Q&A all-correct rises with N and shows no conjunctive/disjunctive drop. Normalised exploration efficiency: gpt-4o conj -1.444 (sd 3.109), deepseek-reasoner conj -1.881 (sd 6.509), gpt-4o-mini conj 0.319 (sd 1.255). Oracle-explored data: only deepseek-reasoner near perfect.
limits: No equal-token comparison between the sampling agent and plain or reasoning baselines. The paper's own conclusion says future work should test generalisation beyond Blicket tests and combination with other reasoning techniques. Sampling agent shown on one model. Authors guess that reasoning amplifies the disjunctive prior; this is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: in the source there is no equal-token test and no non-blicket task. Also a warning that adding reasoning tokens alone may not fix exploration.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) appendix C.5 - hypothesis-sampling agent prompts
finding: The sampling agent asks for N python hypotheses, deletes any that fail past observations, and asks the model for an action that eliminates the most. The generation prompt already limits hypotheses to the two forms 'one blicket suffices' or 'all blickets needed', with boolean operations only. So the scaffold also lists the rule forms.
numbers: Elimination needs exact match to all past observations (f(x_i)=y_i for all i). Duplicates rejected. No sampling temperature or token counts in the appendix text read.
limits: This confounds two ingredients: sampling many hypotheses and telling the model which rule forms exist. No ablation separating them was seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the scaffold's gain cannot be credited to sampling alone. Our test should run 'list rule forms only' vs 'sample N hypotheses only' vs both.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik & Precup (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists (arXiv 2606.06464, CogSci 2026) - model results
finding: Six LLMs (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, o4-mini, deepseek-chat) played the 4-object blicket task actively. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner reached near-perfect disjunctive accuracy, and gpt-5 came close to average adult accuracy in conjunctive too. Models still needed more tests for conjunctive rules.
numbers: 24 trials per rule per model, 288 LLM trials, temperature 0. Humans N=306 (102 active, 102 passive observers, 102 passive proposers). Mean tests, conjunctive vs disjunctive: humans 9.6 vs 6.4; gpt-5 10.2 vs 7.7; gpt-5-mini 10.8 vs 7.1; gemini-2.5-flash 13.5 vs 9.71; deepseek-reasoner 8.2 vs 6.8; o4-mini 6.7 vs 4.2; deepseek-chat 12.3 vs 11.9. Human object-ID accuracy by mode: active 0.69, passive observer 0.45, passive proposer 0.12.
limits: Same research circle as GX-Chen. The task lets models know the rule could be conjunctive or disjunctive. Exploration vs evidence reading not separated. Per-model final accuracies sit in a figure whose text extraction was garbled, so they are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly answered: for the strongest 2025 reasoning models with the rule forms named, the conjunctive accuracy handicap mostly closes, but the extra test cost remains (about 30-45% more tests for most models).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky & Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models (arXiv 2604.02485)
finding: Prompting for opposite or falsifying tests raised rule discovery in Wason-style triples and in a new blicket task. Thinking-mode models used more tokens per turn under the intervention. Distilling the behaviour into a smaller model transferred partly to blicket.
numbers: Eleven LLMs, success 6% to 78% within 45 turns; interventions raise discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Human baseline N=29, 21 found the rule; incompatible-to-compatible ratio 1.79 for first-try success vs 0.24. Think-in-Opposites tokens per turn, thinking mode: Qwen3-8B 1088 to 1716, Qwen3-14B 1179 to 1332, Qwen3-32B 1030 to 1450, R1-Llama-70B 958 to 1073. Non-thinking models: effect small or mixed. Blicket (192 episodes per point): Qwen3-32B 0.57 to 0.86 with TiO, ratio 0.54 to 1.31; Qwen3-8B 0.32 to 0.40.
limits: Only Qwen3, QwQ, Llama-3.3, R1-distill and GPT-4o family; no frontier 2026 model. Not matched on tokens: the intervention adds 12-58% tokens in thinking models. Falsification needed a reformulation for blicket. One author is on the GX-Chen team.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly answered: forcing a falsifying test helps most for thinking models, costs roughly 12-58% more tokens per turn, and does not reliably help non-thinking models. No evidence outside rule-discovery games.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen & van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2503.17523) - appendix B and prompt-level checks
finding: Without fine-tuning, a hybrid helps: ask the LLM for its verbalised beliefs about the user, then let an external symbolic step choose. That beats the LLM's direct choice. Chain-of-thought, a numeric (not text) encoding of the options, and 30 rounds instead of 5 did not fix belief updating.
numbers: Closed models were Gemini 1.5 Pro and GPT-4.1 Mini; open models Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5. Direct and belief-derived predictions agree less than 50% of the time for original LLMs. Bayesian assistant 81% final-round accuracy. Numeric representation did no better than text. 30 rounds: Gemma Original not better.
limits: Flight-recommendation preference task, not rule discovery. No 2025-26 reasoning model tested. The external step used verbalised beliefs, not a belief table the LLM updates by code. Fine-tuned models still best.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 mostly open: no source tests a code-updated numeric belief table at inference time. A hybrid that keeps the arithmetic outside the LLM is only weakly supported (beats direct LLM choice, still below fine-tuned).

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, Bhatia, Li, Bhaskar, Zaman & Goodman (2025) BoxingGym (arXiv 2501.01540) - prior vs no prior
finding: Giving domain context did not help and often hurt. The authors give the cause: the model fixes an overly strong assumption early and does not revise it. In hyperbolic discounting, error rose with more experiments.
numbers: Six LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, Qwen-2.5-32B and 7B, OpenThinker-32B and 7B); 5 runs; evaluation after 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 10 experiments. EI regret compares the chosen experiment's expected information gain to the best of 100 random ones. Qwen2.5 instruct models beat OpenThinker reasoning models in Fig 3b.
limits: Metrics are prediction error and EI regret, not a direct count of test diversity. So the claim that a stated prior reduces test diversity is not measured. Small N (5 runs).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: stated context can anchor via a held assumption, not shown via narrow tests. To test: label the stated prior as revisable and trigger a re-test on surprise.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu & Xing (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning (arXiv 2604.20039), independent group
finding: Extended blicket benchmark with a mid-episode rule switch, run with Claude Sonnet 4.5. The plain agent already reached 87.3% raw accuracy when the task text named both candidate rule types. A context-graph scaffold alone was lower (77.3%). Only the combination with runtime monitors was nominally best (89.1%).
numbers: Pooled 110 episodes per agent (Runs 03, 04, 06). Base 96/110 (87.3%), CG 85/110 (77.3%), CG+DB 98/110 (89.1%). Among episodes where reasoning was eligible: 97.5% (79/81), 98.7%, 97.9%. 1,085 episodes in the main series cost about $807; $0.17 to $3.16 per episode; CG+DB costs 30-50% more than Base at matched step budgets. Temperature 1.0.
limits: CG+DB vs CG p=0.015 is one-tailed and post hoc; Base vs CG+DB (87.3 vs 89.1) is not shown to differ. Not a replication of the disjunctive bias; rule types were given in the prompt. Company-affiliated authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly closed: an independent group used a blicket variant with a frontier model. When rule forms are listed, the plain agent is already strong, which supports 'list the rule forms' as a cheap fix (gap 2) and warns that extra structure can hurt.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2402.06025)
finding: LLM-proposed natural-language hypotheses tracked as weighted particles (sequential Monte Carlo), plus choosing the experiment that best splits them, beat an LLM-only ReAct-style agent on Zendo. Information-gain choice beat random choice and beat asking the LLM to pick the experiment.
numbers: Zendo test score (out of 8, 5 seeds): human 5.26; direct LLM (ReAct) 4.60; online fuzzy 6.01; strongest model 6.55 (+/- 0.13). Experiment choice with online hard rules: LLM-chosen 4.72, random 5.84, InfoGain 6.55. ActiveACRE task-solving: best model 0.35 vs 0.00 to 0.15 for others. GPT-4 Turbo for hypotheses, GPT-3.5 for code. Human-model fit shows an inverted U in LLM calls per iteration.
limits: Cornell/Google group, 2024 models, Zendo not blicket. The InfoGain score was computed by program, not by prompt. Table columns were garbled in extraction, so batch/online assignments of some cells are unsure; the 4.60, 5.26, 6.55 and Table 3 values are clear.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: tracking several weighted hypotheses, not just the best one, is what lets the agent choose a discriminating test. Gap 1: a test chosen by code-computed information gain beat one chosen by the LLM by 1.8 of 8 points.

source: Jiang & Lucas (2024) Actively learning to learn causal relationships (PMC13292816)
finding: Adults who first learned one rule form (disjunctive or conjunctive) transfer it to the next task, but a mismatch hurts mainly when the next task is disjunctive, and many adults ignore the earlier task.
numbers: Exp1 N=212 (181 after filter), 8 conditions; disjunctive transfer matched vs mismatched: long training p=.051, short p=.078 (full data), p=.035 and p=.017 (filtered). Conjunctive matched vs mismatched n.s. First intervention uses more blocks after conjunctive training, t(183.39)=4.62, p<.001. Conjunctive transfer harder overall, z=4.26. Exp2 N=250: average predictive likelihood No-Transfer .059, full hierarchical .055, fixed-form .018, random .016.
limits: Only the first 100000 of 163769 characters read; per-condition means were not in that part. Many people look like no-transfer. Adults, not agents.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: cross-task rule-form memory can help but costs when forms differ, and many learners behave as if there is no transfer. Keep it as a soft prior that re-opens on surprise.

source: Jin et al. (2023/24) CLadder Table 2, rung accuracy for seeing vs doing
finding: Vanilla GPT-4 scored about the same on rung 1 (seeing) and rung 2 (doing). CausalCoT lifted rung 1 much more than rung 2.
numbers: GPT-4 vanilla: overall 62.03, rung1 63.01, rung2 62.82, rung3 60.55. CausalCoT: overall 70.40, rung1 83.35, rung2 67.47, rung3 62.05. Random about 50 per rung.
limits: Row assignment read from a garbled table; overall values (62.03, 70.40) match the paper's prose, rung values should be checked in the PDF. 2023 model. No 2025-26 test of a Waldmann-type seeing-versus-doing task was found.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for 2025-26. The 2023-24 data do not show a clear see/do gap on templated text questions; this is not the same as Waldmann's chain tasks.

source: Semantic Scholar index check for 'blicket detector language models' (query run 2026-11-01)
finding: Of the top 15 results for the query (limit 15, years 2023-2026), exactly one is a blicket-plus-LLM paper (Samiei 2026, 0 citations). The other 14 are unrelated detector papers. Other searches were rate-limited. This is a weak negative signal only.
numbers: 1 of 15 results relevant; the hit has 0 citations. The first-pass search (no year filter) also returned Samiei 2026 as the only blicket-LLM hit in 25 results.
limits: Search index and keyword match are crude; GX-Chen 2025, Jhaveri 2026 and Alderete 2026 do not use 'blicket detector' in the title so would not appear. Web search budget was exhausted; arXiv and OpenAlex were rate-limited (HTTP 429) at the time.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: nothing found that independently reproduces GX-Chen's conjunctive bias on LLMs; Alderete 2026 and Jhaveri 2026 use blickets for other aims.
